analysis.one_liner: Creates a mandatory federal inspection and certification program for all fish and seafood sold in the U.S.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after one subcommittee hearing in November 1989, it sat in three House committees until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every processing plant and fishing vessel selling seafood in interstate commerce to hold a federal certificate, pass unannounced inspections, follow sanitation and handling standards, and use truthful labeling — with fines, public naming of violators, and felony penalties for intentional adulteration. Imported seafood would have had to meet the same rules or come from countries with approved safety programs. It died in committee without a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who eat seafood that today is inspected far less rigorously than meat or poultry. The bill targeted contaminants (chemicals, bacteria, natural toxins like ciguatoxin), filthy processing conditions, and misleading labels — risks the bill text notes are heightened because fish come from polluted waters, spoil fast, and are often eaten raw. It also protects honest seafood businesses from undercutting by violators, and protects workers who report safety problems.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every establishment and vessel processing seafood for interstate commerce to hold an official certificate and submit to inspection at any time, unannounced, day or night [S3].
Deems seafood adulterated if it contains hazardous substances, comes from polluted shellfish beds, or is imported from a country without an approved safety program [S3].

Imposes a $10,000 fine per violation (rising 5% for repeat offenses), publicly names violators in the Federal Register, and makes intentional adulteration a felony carrying up to two years in prison [S3].
Bars employers from firing or punishing workers who assist in carrying out the Act [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Seafood processors, fishing vessels, and importers, who would bear the cost of certification, inspections, sanitation upgrades, recordkeeping, and the risk of fines and certificate suspensions — costs likely passed partly to consumers in higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on fishing vessels and small processing plants, and some of that cost would reach consumers through higher seafood prices [S3].
The bill concentrates sweeping power in the Secretary of Agriculture — including summarily suspending certificates and withholding labels — with only after-the-fact hearings and judicial review [S3].
It authorizes $75 million per year in new appropriations for four fiscal years, a real cost to taxpayers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is broad but hard to price: mandatory inspection would catch contaminated and mishandled seafood before it reaches stores, in a sector the bill's own findings call under-inspected relative to meat and poultry. The costs — industry compliance and $75 million a year in appropriations — are real but modest next to the scale of the program. The main design weakness is the concentration of enforcement power in one Cabinet secretary with limited upfront due process.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three different House committees, then to three subcommittees, got a single hearing in November 1989, and was never brought up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Introduced September 28, 1989 by Rep. Dan Glickman of Kansas, with Reps. George Brown of California and Jim Jontz, and referred jointly to the Energy and Commerce, Merchant Marine and Fisheries, and Agriculture committees [S1][S3].
It was split among three subcommittees — Department Operations, Fisheries and Wildlife, and Health and the Environment — and executive comments were requested from USDA, Commerce, and HHS [S5].
A subcommittee hearing was held on November 9, 1989, but no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever followed [S5].
The bill drew only two cosponsors in its two years of life [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Seafood processors, fishing vessels, and importers came out ahead: they avoided certification, inspection, and recordkeeping costs, and the government avoided a new $75-million-a-year program. Consumers continued to buy seafood under the weaker, voluntary inspection system the bill's findings called insufficient.

against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up after referral; no markup or committee vote appears in its history.

against.role: Processors, fishing vessels, and importers facing new regulation

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats, and the bill's only cosponsors were two of the 257 House Democrats [S4]; no Republican support appears anywhere in the record.

industries.note: The bill would require certification, sanitation upgrades, unannounced inspections, and public recordkeeping, with fines for violations. Those are costs to the industry and safeguards for consumers, so the industry's interest in killing the bill ran against the public's interest in safer seafood.
Imports could be barred unless they met U.S. standards or came from a country with an approved safety program. Compliance costs would fall on importers while the protection went to consumers.

An official stamp available only to certified establishments would reward firms already meeting high standards and help them against violators, whose identities the bill would publish in the Federal Register.
